posts.cooked:
I just found myself thinking about how I was looking forward to the putative future electronic version of Sentinels of the Multiverse because then if I was uncertain what the resolution would be to some part of the game I could just see how the electronic version handled it. It then occurred to me that it would also be really cool if the putative future electronic version kept a log of the game state such that the log could be loaded in at some point in the future and one could scroll forward and backward in the log and see everything that happened. So, requests:

 

1) Make the game such that one can specify a game state (decks, cards in hand, cards in play, cards in trash, HP, etc.).

2) Make the game such that there is a log of what happens in the game, that the log is saveable, and that the log is loadable.

3) Make the game such that one can step backwards and forwards through the log of a game.

 

Are these the most important things for the game? No. Much more important would be making sure that the game is correct, easy to use, and fun to play. Still, the items above would be really cool to have.

posts.name: Mezike
posts.cooked:
Multiplayer would be very very cool, but it may be lacking without voice capability. What makes face to face, forum, and Google+ games so enjoyable is being able to talk strategy while we play. And, also, just to talk while we play, Sentinels players being the sociable bunch that we are

I guess that the Villain and Enviro decks would be automated so the setup would either be multiple players connecting to a central server, or one player hosting a game that the others connect to - i'm not going to pretend I have the first clue as to which is better or more achievable!

I think another neat idea would be to add scalable difficulty with a menu of additional advanced modes for villains, e.g. so that you can change H-1 to H, or start Baron Blade with cards discarded into his trash. These sorts of things would be easy enough to implement in a digital format, although for sure it wouldn't be in tune with the physical game.

posts.name: Rabk

Silverleaf:

I also prefer paper books (and own many of them) but I can't argue with the convenience and portability of my basic no-bells-and-whistles Kindle. Unexpectedly finishing a book 10 minutes into a long journey isn't a problem now because I have several hundred others available in the one device.And putting a couple of hundred or so of my less precious physical books into storge in the loft has left me with more shelf space for board games (and let's face it, more books) which is never a bad thing.

Speaking as someone with hundreds of cubic feet of storage space occupied by physical books and games, the idea of freeing room to make things more accessible when needed is an amazing one. The convienience of not lugging piles of paper and cardboard along on our daily commutes also can't be discounted; we simply spend too much time away from our collections/libraries to rely on physical copies 100% of the time.

That being said, the physical act of sliding a freshly-shuffled deck of cards to your friend across the table or of hearing the pages ruffle open when slipping your bookmark out from between them cannot possibly be matched in any digital medium. I may opt to save my back and bring the tablet along on a long flight, but it will never be a replacement for the smell of lignin or the sound of meeple stacking atop one another once I'm back home.
